stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many analysts assume that workers who change employers often early in their careers pay a price in slower wage growth. Labor economist Mireille Hauser's analysis of payroll records complicates that view. She found that workers who changed employers at least twice in their first five years were disproportionately concentrated in software and logistics. In those two sectors, she also found, wages during the first decade of a career grew faster than the national average for all sectors. Hauser's findings therefore indicate that frequent early job changers ______
choices: earn more over their careers than do workers who remain with one employer
are overrepresented in sectors where early-career wages have grown faster than average
make up the majority of all workers employed in the software and logistics sectors
confirm the assumption that frequent job changes early on slow a worker's wage growth
explanation: The shared term is 'software and logistics.' Fact 1: frequent early job changers are disproportionately found in those sectors. Fact 2: those sectors had faster-than-average early-career wage growth. Remove the shared term and you get the link: frequent early job changers are overrepresented in sectors with faster-than-average early-career wage growth. This choice adds nothing beyond the two facts.

A.why: You went past the chain. Hauser describes the sectors, not individual lifetime earnings, and she never compares job changers with workers who stay at one employer. That comparison needs an extra step the passage doesn't give you.

C.why: You turned 'disproportionately concentrated' into 'the majority,' which is strength creep, and you also flipped the direction. The passage says a large share of job changers work in these sectors. It doesn't say job changers make up most of each sector's workforce.

D.why: The passage says Hauser's findings 'complicate' the analysts' assumption. You picked the view the passage is undercutting, not the corrected view the blank should finish.

rated_why: understand evidence and scope: changers concentrated in high-growth sectors, but this doesn't prove they earn more overall

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Nineteenth-century lithographers printing in color needed a separate printing surface for each hue, and because limestone of lithographic quality came almost entirely from quarries near Solnhofen, Bavaria, large color editions were costly to produce elsewhere. In the 1870s some printers adopted zinc plates, which could be grained to hold a greasy image much as limestone did. Unlike Solnhofen stone, zinc could be manufactured in quantity by foundries in many countries. Printers who replaced stones with zinc plates were therefore able to ______
choices: print every hue of a color edition from a single grained zinc plate
produce color prints of finer quality than Solnhofen stone could yield
make color editions without relying on stone from Bavarian quarries
obtain lithographic limestone from foundries in a number of countries
explanation: The passage names the flaw: color printing needed many surfaces, and the only suitable stone came from Bavaria. Zinc holds an image the way limestone does, so it can replace the stone. It is also made in many countries. Link these facts and printers using zinc could make color editions without depending on Bavarian quarries. That fixes exactly the problem the passage described.

A.why: The passage says each hue needed its own printing surface, and nothing suggests zinc changed that. Zinc replaced the material, not the number of surfaces. This choice goes against a stated fact.

B.why: The passage says zinc worked 'much as limestone did.' It says nothing about zinc being better. You added a quality comparison the text never makes.

D.why: You merged the two facts incorrectly. Foundries make zinc, not limestone. This choice uses the words from the passage but misattributes where each material comes from.

rated_why: two steps with plausible wrong answers: identify Solnhofen as bottleneck, then recognize zinc breaks that dependence

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In field trials, agronomist Tomás Ferreira's team found that planting cowpeas between rows of sorghum left sorghum grain yields unchanged but sharply reduced infestations of stem borer larvae in the sorghum plants. In an earlier study, the team had shown that feeding damage from stem borers is the main route by which fungi enter sorghum grain, leading to contamination during storage. Ferreira's findings therefore suggest that interplanting sorghum with cowpeas may ______
choices: lower fungal contamination in stored sorghum without reducing the size of the harvest
raise sorghum grain yields by protecting the plants from stem borer feeding damage
eliminate fungal contamination from stored sorghum grain regardless of other conditions
reduce the share of stored cowpea grain that becomes contaminated by fungi
explanation: The shared term is stem borers. Interplanting reduces stem borers, and stem borer damage is the main way fungi get into stored sorghum. Link the two and interplanting may lower fungal contamination. The first study also says yield stayed the same, so this happens without shrinking the harvest. The choice uses both parts of the split result.

B.why: You focused on the half of the result that changed (fewer borers) and missed the half that held steady. The passage says yields were 'unchanged,' so a yield increase goes against the text.

C.why: This is strength creep. Borer damage is the 'main' route for fungi, not the only one, and the passage only says 'may.' 'Eliminate ... regardless of other conditions' claims far more than the chain supports.

D.why: You attached the finding to the wrong crop. Every fact about borers and fungal contamination is about sorghum. The cowpeas are only the intervention.

rated_why: causal chain across studies: fewer borers → less fungal entry, paired with yield unchanged

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Scholars have often attributed the unusually wide vocal ranges of the songs of fourteenth-century composer Aldric of Tours to the exceptional singers at the court where he worked. Musicologist Hanne Vestergaard notes, however, that every surviving copy of Aldric's widest-ranging songs belongs to a set of manuscripts prepared for use at Rouen Cathedral. Rouen's records, she adds, show that the cathedral's singers routinely divided a song between two voices, one taking the low passages and the other the high. Vestergaard's observations suggest that Aldric's widest-ranging songs ______
choices: were never performed by the singers at the court where Aldric worked
may not have required any one singer to cover their full vocal range
confirm that Aldric's court employed singers of unusual vocal ability
were originally composed for performance by the singers of Rouen
explanation: The shared term is Rouen Cathedral. The songs survive only in manuscripts prepared for use at Rouen, and Rouen routinely split songs between a low singer and a high singer. Link the two and the songs may have been divided, so no single singer needed the whole range. The word 'suggest' allows only a hedged conclusion like 'may not have required.'

A.why: The passage only tells you where the surviving copies were used. It says nothing that rules out performances at court. 'Never' is strength creep beyond the evidence.

C.why: The word 'however' marks Vestergaard's point as a challenge to the court-singer explanation. You picked the popular view the passage undercuts.

D.why: You treated 'prepared for use at Rouen' as if it meant 'composed for Rouen.' Copying a song for a place is not the same as writing it for that place. That step isn't in the passage.

rated_why: counterargument logic: wide range explained by splitting singers, not exceptional ability—requires reading against initial assumption

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Sprinters often post faster times after training camps at high altitude, and coaches commonly credit the thin air. Physiologist Ren Kato's study of national-team sprinters found that post-camp gains in sprint speed were closely associated with increases in athletes' nightly sleep. Kato also found that athletes slept substantially more at the camps than during training at home, likely because the camps freed them from commuting and work obligations. Kato's results thus suggest that the improvement coaches observe ______
choices: comes from altitude and would occur no matter how much athletes slept
has nothing to do with the reduced oxygen available at high altitude
would be even greater for distance runners than it is for sprinters
may owe something to added sleep at the camps and not only to altitude
explanation: The shared term is sleep. Speed gains are associated with more sleep, and the camps produce more sleep. Link the two and the camps' extra sleep may explain part of the improvement. Kato only raises sleep as another explanation, so the evidence is inconclusive about altitude. It doesn't disprove altitude, which is why the answer is hedged with 'may' and 'not only.'

A.why: Kato found the gains were closely tied to sleep. Saying they would happen 'no matter how much athletes slept' goes against that finding and repeats the coaches' view.

B.why: This is the hedge trap. Kato's results raise another explanation. They don't prove that altitude plays no role. 'Nothing to do with' treats a possible alternative as if it disproved altitude.

C.why: The study covered only sprinters. A comparison with distance runners goes beyond the chain and applies the sample to a group that wasn't studied.

rated_why: distinguish what evidence rules out: correlation with sleep doesn't eliminate altitude, but suggests both matter

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Stomata are pores through which leaves take in carbon dioxide, and in living plants, stomatal density tends to rise when atmospheric carbon dioxide is scarce. At a fossil site in Wyoming, leaves of the extinct plant Vellaria occur in a sequence of rock layers spanning roughly two million years. Leaves from the older, lower layers have relatively few stomata, whereas leaves from the younger, upper layers have markedly more. If Vellaria responded to carbon dioxide as living plants do, these findings suggest that atmospheric carbon dioxide ______
choices: probably declined over the period in which the site's rock layers formed
rose steadily over the period in which the site's rock layers formed
declined at the same rate worldwide as it did near the Wyoming site
fell sharply enough to cause Vellaria's extinction after the upper layers formed
explanation: The shared term is stomatal density. More stomata go with scarcer carbon dioxide, and stomata increased from the older layers to the younger ones. Link the two and carbon dioxide probably fell over the time the layers record. The passage's 'if' and 'suggest' only allow 'probably,' and nothing reaches beyond this one site.

B.why: You reversed the relationship. Higher stomatal density goes with less carbon dioxide, not more. So rising density points to falling carbon dioxide.

C.why: The evidence comes from one site. Claiming the same rate worldwide applies a local finding to the whole globe, which the chain doesn't support.

D.why: The passage never explains why Vellaria went extinct. Linking the carbon dioxide drop to extinction adds a causal step that no fact provides.

rated_why: inverse relationship: more stomata over time plus rule about scarcity requires concluding CO₂ declined

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Some astronomers have argued that the reddish surfaces of certain small icy bodies indicate that the bodies formed beyond Neptune. Laboratory experiments show that such reddening occurs when methanol-rich ice is exposed to radiation for long periods. Planetary scientist Inês Albuquerque points out, however, that methanol-rich ice forms only where temperatures are extremely low, and that models of the early solar system place such conditions not only beyond Neptune but also in a zone just outside Saturn's orbit. Albuquerque's point implies that a reddish surface ______
choices: shows that a body must have formed in the zone just outside Saturn's orbit
results from exposure to radiation rather than from methanol-rich ice
is more common among bodies from near Saturn than among bodies from beyond Neptune
does not by itself establish that a body formed beyond Neptune rather than near Saturn
explanation: The chain runs like this: reddening comes from methanol-rich ice, and that ice could form in two regions, beyond Neptune and near Saturn. So a reddish surface fits either birthplace. It can't settle the question alone. Albuquerque only opens a second possibility, so the correct choice says the evidence is inconclusive rather than naming a winner.

A.why: This is the hedge trap. Albuquerque shows that the Saturn zone is possible, not that it's certain. 'Must have formed' swaps one unsupported certainty for another.

B.why: The experiments show that reddening needs both radiation and methanol-rich ice. Setting them against each other with 'rather than' goes against the lab result.

C.why: The passage gives no frequencies for either region. Comparing how common reddish bodies are adds a claim that neither fact supports.

rated_why: complex evidence logic: methanol ice can form in two places, so reddish surface alone cannot distinguish origin

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Historians have often assumed that the blue woolens recovered from medieval graves at the Danish trading town of Ribe were colored with woad, a dye plant grown locally. Chemical analysis by textile historian Signe Madsen, however, found pigment ratios in the fibers characteristic of indigo from tropical Indigofera plants, which cannot be cultivated in Scandinavia. Madsen also notes that in that period, tropical goods reached northern Europe only by way of Byzantine markets. Madsen's findings thus suggest that the dye on the Ribe woolens ______
choices: was made from woad grown in the fields surrounding the town of Ribe
was the same dye used on all blue textiles in medieval Scandinavia
reached northern Europe through trade passing through Byzantine markets
was more costly than any other dye available in medieval Europe
explanation: The shared term is tropical goods. The dye came from tropical Indigofera, and tropical goods reached northern Europe only through Byzantine markets. Link the two and the dye must have come north through Byzantine trade. This choice states that link and nothing more.

A.why: This is the old view that the word 'however' sets aside. Madsen's analysis points to tropical indigo, not local woad.

B.why: Madsen analyzed woolens from one town's graves. 'All blue textiles in medieval Scandinavia' stretches that sample into a claim about every case.

D.why: The passage never mentions price. You assumed that long-distance trade makes a dye the most expensive, which is an extra step the text doesn't take.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Two-step chain requiring careful reading to reject answer contradicting the evidence
